easy.explanation: He says, “I am the man that hath seen affliction.”
easy.q: What does the speaker say he has seen?

easy.explanation: The KJV says, “He hath led me, and brought me into darkness.”
easy.q: Where has the speaker been led?

answers: His flesh and skin grew old, and his bones were broken
easy.explanation: His flesh and skin were made old, and his bones were broken.
easy.q: What happened to the speaker’s body?

answers: He is left isolated and desolate
medium.explanation: His ways are enclosed, his paths are crooked, and he is made desolate.
medium.q: What is the result of the speaker’s ways being enclosed?

answers: A gate was opened for him
He was blocked in and could not escape
medium.explanation: The words describe being surrounded and unable to get out.
medium.q: What does “he hath hedged me about, that I cannot get out” mean?

answers: From the body to a celebration
From darkness to injury, confinement, and desolation
medium.explanation: The passage moves from darkness and bodily pain to blocked paths and desolation.
medium.q: How do the descriptions of suffering build in this passage?

answers: A sense of lost direction and distress
challenge.explanation: Darkness represents the speaker’s distress and lack of light or direction.
challenge.q: What does the image of darkness emphasize?

answers: That the speaker is completely free
That trouble surrounds him on every side
That the speaker is at a feast
challenge.explanation: These images portray confinement, heaviness, and the absence of an easy escape.
challenge.q: What do the images of walls, heavy chains, and crooked paths suggest?

challenge.explanation: “Desolate” summarizes the speaker’s loneliness and ruin.
challenge.q: What feeling is created by the ending, “he hath made me desolate”?

easy.explanation: He says that God has set him “as a mark for the arrow.”
easy.q: What is the speaker compared to in verse 12?

answers: He becomes their derision and song
easy.explanation: He says, “I was a derision to all my people; and their song all the day.”
easy.q: How do the speaker’s people treat him?

easy.explanation: Bitterness, wormwood, mockery, and suffering lead him to say that his hope has perished.
easy.q: What affects the speaker’s hope?

medium.explanation: The arrow is an image of the painful injuries the speaker experiences.
medium.q: What connection is there between the arrow and the wounds described in the passage?

medium.explanation: Wormwood is a bitter substance used here as a picture of painful experience.
medium.q: What does “wormwood” represent in this passage?

answers: Because he has found an open path
medium.explanation: The continuing arrows, bitterness, and ridicule overwhelm his hope.
medium.q: Why does the speaker feel that hope has perished?

answers: Suffering is shown as both physical injury and inward bitterness
challenge.explanation: Arrows portray bodily pain, while wormwood portrays the bitter inner experience of suffering.
challenge.q: What is the significance of moving from arrows to wormwood?

answers: That the mockery and suffering seemed continuous
challenge.explanation: The phrase stresses the ongoing nature of the people’s ridicule.
challenge.q: What does “all the day” emphasize?

answers: It expresses the speaker’s feeling that his future and hope are gone
challenge.explanation: The statement summarizes the speaker’s deep discouragement after prolonged suffering.
challenge.q: How does “my strength and my hope is perished” relate to the passage?

easy.explanation: He remembers his affliction, misery, wormwood, and gall.
easy.q: What does the speaker remember at the beginning of this section?

easy.explanation: He says, “This I recall to my mind, therefore have I hope,” referring to the LORD’S mercies.
easy.q: What does he recall to his mind?

easy.explanation: The passage says, “They are new every morning.”
easy.q: What is new every morning?

answers: It moves him from despair toward hope
It makes him happy without reflection
It causes him to forget everything
medium.explanation: Remembering the LORD’S mercies gives him hope despite his affliction.
medium.q: How does remembering change the speaker’s attitude?

answers: The LORD’S mercies are renewed each morning
medium.explanation: The phrase describes God’s compassion as continually renewed.
medium.q: What does “They are new every morning” mean?

answers: Because the LORD is his portion and remains faithful
medium.explanation: The LORD’S mercies, compassions, and faithfulness give him reason to hope.
medium.q: Why does the speaker say, “therefore will I hope in him”?

answers: The tension between remembered suffering and awakened hope
The tension between a feast and a celebration
The tension between light and happiness only
challenge.explanation: The section begins with painful memories but turns toward mercy, faithfulness, and hope.
challenge.q: What is the central tension in this section?

answers: To trust God patiently and silently
challenge.explanation: The verse joins patient waiting with confidence in the LORD’S salvation.
challenge.q: What does it mean to “hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD”?

answers: There is no value in learning patience
Youth is only a time for pleasure
Bearing difficulty can teach a person while he is young
challenge.explanation: The verse presents carrying a yoke in youth as a beneficial discipline.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from “It is good for a man that he bear the yoke in his youth”?

paragraphs.title: Bearing the Yoke and Trusting Divine Justice

easy.explanation: The passage says, “He sitteth alone and keepeth silence.”
easy.q: What should a person do when bearing the yoke?

answers: He will not cast off forever
easy.explanation: Verse 31 says, “For the Lord will not cast off for ever.”
easy.q: What does the passage say about the Lord?

easy.explanation: The passage asks why a living man should complain “for the punishment of his sins.”
easy.q: What should a person consider at the end of the section?

medium.explanation: The speaker presents quiet endurance as the proper response to the yoke.
medium.q: How are silence and bearing the yoke related?

medium.explanation: A yoke is a burden, representing the difficulty a person must bear.
medium.q: What does “yoke” mean in this context?

answers: God does not willingly afflict or approve injustice, and people must face their sins
medium.explanation: The passage says God does not afflict willingly and does not approve turning aside a person’s right.
medium.q: How does the passage present divine justice?

answers: It leaves room for hope amid suffering
It removes every possibility of hope
It describes a victory already achieved
challenge.explanation: Even in humiliation and suffering, the words leave open the possibility of hope.
challenge.q: What role does “if so be there may be hope” play in the passage?

answers: It explains and supports the speaker’s claims
It changes to an unrelated subject
challenge.explanation: The statements give reasons concerning God’s mercy, justice, and human responsibility.
challenge.q: What does the repeated reasoning in this section accomplish?

answers: Compassion removes the need for self-examination
Confidence in mercy allows a person to face sin without despair
challenge.explanation: The LORD is compassionate, yet the passage still calls people to recognize the punishment of their sins.
challenge.q: What is the relationship between God’s compassion and acknowledging sin?

easy.explanation: They are told, “Let us search and try our ways.”
easy.q: What are the people told to do?

easy.explanation: The people are told to “turn again to the LORD.”
easy.q: To whom should they return?

easy.explanation: The verse says, “Let us lift up our heart with our hands unto God.”
easy.q: What do they lift up to God?

answers: Examining their ways, returning, and confessing rebellion
medium.explanation: The people examine their ways, turn to the LORD, and confess that they have transgressed and rebelled.
medium.q: What order of actions does the passage recommend?

medium.explanation: The expression describes offering the heart to God in repentance and prayer.
medium.q: What does “lift up our heart” mean in this context?

answers: It moves from confession to anger, blocked prayer, and humiliation
medium.explanation: After confession, the passage describes persecution, a covering cloud, and disgrace among the people.
medium.q: How does the tone change from self-examination to the people’s cry?

answers: The call is addressed to the people as a group
The speaker is talking only about himself
The speaker is addressing the enemies
challenge.explanation: The plural language presents repentance as a communal act.
challenge.q: What does the repeated use of “Let us” suggest?

answers: Confession appears alongside the experience of judgment and distance from God
Confession ends the need to cry out
challenge.explanation: The people confess their rebellion and then describe anger, persecution, and prayer that cannot pass through.
challenge.q: How are “We have transgressed and have rebelled” and blocked prayer related?

answers: A sense of distance and no response
challenge.explanation: The cloud symbolizes a barrier between the people’s prayer and God.
challenge.q: What does the image of a cloud preventing prayer emphasize?

answers: For the destruction of the daughter of his people
easy.explanation: His eye runs down with water because of the destruction of his people.
easy.q: Why does the speaker weep?

answers: From the top of a mountain
easy.explanation: He calls upon the LORD “out of the low dungeon.”
easy.q: From where does the speaker call upon the LORD?

answers: He hears, draws near, and says, “Fear not”
easy.explanation: The LORD hears the cry, draws near, and tells him not to fear.
easy.q: What does the LORD do after the speaker calls?

answers: As rivers of water that do not cease
medium.explanation: His eye runs down with rivers of water, and his tears do not cease.
medium.q: How is the intensity of the speaker’s weeping described?

medium.explanation: The phrase means that the speaker’s tears continue without stopping.
medium.q: What does “ceaseth not” mean?

answers: From weeping to joy without prayer
From pursuit and the dungeon to calling, hearing, and the removal of fear
medium.explanation: The passage moves from danger and tears to God’s attentive and reassuring response.
medium.q: What is the main movement in this section?

answers: A cry from a very low and dangerous condition
A call from a place of celebration
A prayer made from complete security
challenge.explanation: The dungeon represents the depth of the speaker’s distress.
challenge.q: What does “out of the low dungeon” communicate?

answers: The waters represent danger, while the LORD brings nearness and reassurance
challenge.explanation: The waters overwhelm the speaker, but the LORD draws near and says, “Fear not.”
challenge.q: How does the contrast between threatening waters and the LORD’S voice function?

answers: The speaker never calls upon the LORD
Calling in distress brings a sense of the LORD’S nearness
challenge.explanation: The verse connects the speaker’s cry with the LORD’S drawing near.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from “Thou drewest near in the day that I called upon thee”?

paragraphs.title: Appeal for Judgment against the Enemies

easy.explanation: He says, “O LORD, thou hast seen my wrong.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask the LORD to see?

easy.explanation: The speaker says, “Thou hast heard their reproach, O LORD.”
easy.q: What has the LORD heard?

easy.explanation: He mentions their vengeance, imaginations, reproach, device, and music.
easy.q: What does the speaker describe concerning his enemies?

answers: After being redeemed, he asks the LORD to see the wrong done to him
He stops speaking to the LORD
medium.explanation: After saying that the LORD redeemed his life, he asks God to judge his cause.
medium.q: How does redemption relate to the speaker’s appeal for judgment?

medium.explanation: Those who rose up against him are the people opposing and mocking him.
medium.q: What does “those that rose up against me” refer to?

answers: They repent, become silent, and calm down
They think about him, reproach him, and mock him
medium.explanation: The passage describes their thoughts, reproach, device, and music concerning the speaker.
medium.q: What sequence describes the enemies’ behavior?

answers: The request that the LORD be a full witness to the wrong and mockery
That the speaker does not know what happened
challenge.explanation: The speaker asks the LORD to see, hear, and judge the enemies’ actions.
challenge.q: What does the repeated language of seeing and hearing emphasize?

answers: He leads the enemies in song
He has become an object of their song and mockery
He happily plays music for them
challenge.explanation: The phrase continues the image of the speaker being mocked and made into a song.
challenge.q: What does “I am their musick” mean in context?

answers: Examine the wrong and decide the case
challenge.explanation: The speaker asks the LORD to investigate the wrong and give judgment.
challenge.q: What does the request “judge thou my cause” mean?

paragraphs.title: Retribution and Destruction of the Wicked

answers: A recompence according to their deeds
A reward according to their kindness
A response according to their dreams
easy.explanation: He asks the LORD to repay them according to the work of their hands.
easy.q: What does the speaker ask the LORD to render to the enemies?

easy.explanation: He says, “Give them sorrow of heart.”
easy.q: What does the speaker ask to be given to the enemies’ hearts?

answers: With a blessing for the enemies
With a request that they be pursued and destroyed
easy.explanation: The final verse asks the LORD to pursue and destroy them in anger.
easy.q: How does the section end?

answers: Enemies should receive repayment according to their deeds
medium.explanation: The speaker asks for repayment according to the work of their hands.
medium.q: What principle of retribution appears in this passage?

medium.explanation: The phrase refers to deep inward trouble or grief.
medium.q: What does “sorrow of heart” mean?

answers: From repayment to sorrow, curse, pursuit, and destruction
medium.explanation: The request progresses from recompence to sorrow and curse, ending with pursuit and destruction.
medium.q: How does the severity of the request increase?

answers: It specifies the recompence requested after the appeal for judgment
It cancels the appeal for judgment
It has no relationship to it
challenge.explanation: After asking the LORD to judge his cause, the speaker describes the judgment he desires.
challenge.q: How does this section relate to the preceding appeal for judgment?

answers: The repayment is unrelated to their actions
The repayment should correspond to their deeds
challenge.explanation: The phrase directly connects the requested recompence with their actions.
challenge.q: What does “according to the work of their hands” emphasize?

answers: The enemies are beyond all divine rule
The speaker wants their actions hidden
The speaker asks that they be removed from beneath the LORD’S heavens
challenge.explanation: The ending expresses a request for their removal through divine judgment.
challenge.q: What is suggested by the ending, “from under the heavens of the LORD”?
